extracted.subtask_description: Textbook-style exposition covering reversible/classical and quantum logic gates, Deutsch–Jozsa and Shor algorithms (quantum computing), followed by foundations of real analysis and basic calculus (completeness, sup/inf, sequences, series).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversible gate requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Gates must be reversible, meaning the gates are bijections from the input space to the output space; in particular, such gates must take the same number of input and output bits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: AND, OR, COPY are not reversible for 'dimension reasons'; NOT is reversible (a bijection {0,1}→{0,1}). Reversibility implies we don't need COPY separately in reversible logic constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of reversible simulation / universality (for reversible gates)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of reversible gates can simulate a Boolean function f(x1,...,xn) if one can implement a circuit which takes as input x1,...,xn plus some fixed bits set to 0 or 1 (ancilla bits), and as output returns the original input bits x1,...,xn, the output bit f(x1,...,xn), and possibly some extra bits (garbage bits). The gate(s) are universal if they can simulate any Boolean function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancilla bits are fixed helper bits; garbage bits are allowed in the output. Universality is defined with this reversible simulation model rather than arbitrary erasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNOT limitation: linear functions mod 2 only
rubrics_metrics.description: Any function simulated using only CNOT gates must be of the form a1 x1 + a2 x2 + ... + an xn (mod 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because CNOT acts as (x,y) ↦ (x, x+y), even with ancilla bits we can only create affine linear functions mod 2 (ax + by + c). Hence CNOT alone cannot simulate nonlinear gates like AND.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toffoli (CCNOT) gate definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The three-bit Toffoli gate (CCNOT) maps (x,y,z) ↦ (x,y, z + x y (mod 2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: two control bits toggle the target bit iff both controls are 1. Pictorially depicted with two control dots and a ⊕ on the target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toffoli universality for classical reversible computing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Toffoli gate is universal: it can reversibly simulate AND and NOT (and hence OR), and thus can simulate any Boolean function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: AND implemented with one ancilla bit and no garbage bits; NOT implemented using two ancilla 1 bits and one garbage bit. Universality follows because AND+NOT (or equivalently OR+NOT) suffices to build any Boolean function and these can be implemented reversibly with Toffoli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum gates must be unitary
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantum logic gates are unitary matrices. Equivalently: U preserves inner products (⟨U(x),U(y)⟩ = ⟨x,y⟩), U† is the inverse of U, or ∥x∥ = ∥U(x)∥ for all x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unitary ⇔ reversible in quantum mechanics, so quantum gates always take the same number of input and output qubits. Classical reversible gates have quantum analogs by specifying values on basis elements (e.g., quantum CNOT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled-U gate behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A controlled-U operation applies unitary U to the target register only when the control qubit is |1⟩; otherwise it does nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrammatic behavior: |0⟩ ⊗ |ψ⟩ ↦ |0⟩ ⊗ |ψ⟩, |1⟩ ⊗ |ψ⟩ ↦ |1⟩ ⊗ U|ψ⟩. CNOT is the special case U = σx. If the control is in superposition, applying controlled-U can produce entanglement and nonclassical behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-cloning theorem (quantum)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no unitary map U on two qubits such that U(|ψ⟩ ⊗ |0⟩) = |ψ⟩ ⊗ |ψ⟩ for every qubit |ψ⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: arbitrary quantum states cannot be duplicated. One can copy specific orthogonal basis states (e.g., |0⟩ and |1⟩) via CNOT with a |0⟩ ancilla, but arbitrary superpositions cannot be cloned (entanglement or failure results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deutsch–Jozsa problem setup (oracle model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f: {0,1}^n → {0,1} with the promise that f is either constant or balanced (exactly half outputs 0 and half 1). The function is provided as a reversible black box Uf acting on n+1 qubits: Uf(|x⟩|y⟩) = |x⟩|y + f(x) mod 2⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal: determine whether f is constant or balanced with as few calls to Uf as possible. The slash notation in the diagram indicates an n-qubit register on the top wire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical query complexity for Deutsch–Jozsa
rubrics_metrics.description: Classically, in the worst case one may need up to 2^{n-1} + 1 calls to f to decide whether f is constant or balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the classical baseline of O(2^n) queries; motivates quantum speedup. (Problem statement: show worst-case bound.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deutsch–Jozsa quantum algorithm (one-query solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quantum circuit using Hadamard gates and a single call to Uf can decide the Deutsch–Jozsa promise with one query: prepare |0...0⟩ (top) and |1⟩ (bottom), apply H^⊗n to top and H to bottom, call Uf once, then apply H^⊗n to the top and measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For n=1 explicitly: after the circuit the top qubit is ±|→⟩ if f is constant and ±|←⟩ if f is balanced; measuring in the σx basis (or applying another H and measuring in the computational basis) distinguishes the cases. The output state is not entangled with the bottom qubit and the bottom can be discarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For N=2^n and |ψ⟩ = Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} x_k |k⟩, the QFT is U_QFT(|ψ⟩) = (1/√N) Σ_{j=0}^{N-1} (Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} ω_N^{jk} x_k) |j⟩ where ω_N = exp(2π i / N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a unitary matrix this is the discrete Fourier transform with a normalization factor 1/√N. Proposition: U_QFT(|x_n ... x_1⟩) can be written as a tensor product of single-qubit rotations: ⊗_{t=1}^n (|0⟩ + exp(2π i · 0.x_t...x_1) |1⟩)/√2, which enables an efficient quantum circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient QFT implementation and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: QFT can be implemented using Hadamard gates and controlled phase rotations R_k (with phases exp(2π i / 2^k)), arranged in the standard controlled-R_k pattern followed by swaps; for n qubits this uses O(n^2) gates (i.e., O((log N)^2) when N = 2^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example circuit for n=3 shown; Exercise to verify that the circuit maps |x⟩ to the claimed tensor-product form. This quantum cost is exponentially better than the naive O(N^2) classical matrix multiplication and better than classical FFT's O(N log N) in terms of dependence on N when expressed in n=log N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shor's algorithm reduction: factoring → order-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: To factor M = p q, pick random x modulo M and find the multiplicative order r of x mod M. If x is 'good' (see next criterion), then factors of M can be obtained by computing gcd(x^{r/2} ± 1, M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One shows at least half the residues in (Z/MZ)^× are 'good', so repeated random choices succeed with constant probability; once r is known, gcd computations (Euclidean algorithm) yield nontrivial factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'good' x for Shor's algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: x (mod M) is good if (i) gcd(x,M) = 1, (ii) the order r of x (mod M) is even, and (iii) factoring 0 ≡ (x^{r/2} − 1)(x^{r/2} + 1) (mod M) yields two nonzero factors modulo M (so neither factor is 0 mod M).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these hold, then one of the factors is divisible by p and the other by q, and gcd(x^{r/2} − 1, M) gives a nontrivial factor. Exercise: for M = pq at least half of residues are good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to produce periodic state for order finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick N = 2^n with N ≥ M^2, prepare uniform superposition |ψ⟩ = (1/√N) Σ_{k=0}^{N-1} |k⟩, build circuit U_x which maps |k⟩|0⟩ to |k⟩|x^k mod M⟩, apply U_x to get (1/√N) Σ_k |k⟩|x^k mod M⟩, then measure the second register; the first register collapses to a superposition of basis states spaced by the order r (i.e., a periodic state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring the second register gives a particular residue value and collapses the first to |k0⟩ + |k0 + r⟩ + ... . The (hard) part is constructing U_x efficiently via modular exponentiation by repeated squaring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using QFT and continued fractions to find the order r
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply QFT to the periodically-collapsed first register; measuring yields j such that j r / N is approximately an integer s; using continued fraction expansion on j/N one can recover a candidate s/r and hence r (with some probability of success).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis: the amplitude concentrates on j where ω_N^{j r} ≈ 1, so measured j are close to multiples of N/r. Success probability requires gcd(s,r)=1 (occurs with probability ≈ 1/log r), and multiple trials yield r with high probability. Practical caveats: j=0 yields no information; noise and implementation issues are engineering concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim about quantum factoring complexity (Shor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shor's algorithm can factor M = p q in time roughly O((log M)^2) (the text states O((log M)^2) time for the main quantum steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as the reason for major interest in quantum computing; in practice hidden constants and classical postprocessing (continued fractions, gcd) and error-correction overhead affect real runtimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of R (real numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is complete: as a metric space, sequences converge if and only if they are Cauchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: using supremum of the set S = {x ∈ R | a_n ≥ x for infinitely many n} to define the limit; relies on existence of sup/inf. This property distinguishes R from Q (e.g., limits like 1,1.4,1.41,1.414,... do not converge in Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Least upper bound property (existence of sup/inf)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let S be a nonempty set of real numbers. If S is bounded above then it has a least upper bound (sup S); if S is bounded below then it has a greatest lower bound (inf S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sup(0,1)=1 even though 1∉(0,1). Construction-wise, Dedekind cuts provide a way to construct R and prove this property by taking unions of left halves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone convergence criterion for sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A monotonic bounded sequence (either nonincreasing or nondecreasing and bounded) converges: if a1 ≥ a2 ≥ ... ≥ 0 (monotone decreasing and bounded below) then lim_{n→∞} a_n exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of monotonic given; proof uses completeness or supremum/infimum arguments. Examples illustrate convergence (e.g., decimals truncating to a limit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of limsup and liminf
rubrics_metrics.description: For a sequence (a_n), lim sup_{n→∞} a_n := lim_{N→∞} sup_{n≥N} a_n and lim inf_{n→∞} a_n := lim_{N→∞} inf_{n≥N} a_n (with conventions ±∞ when unbounded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: limsup is 'supremum allowing finitely many terms to be discarded'. Show the tail supremums form a nonincreasing sequence so the limit exists in [−∞,+∞].

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite series convergence via partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite series Σ_k a_k converges to L if the sequence of partial sums s_n = Σ_{k=1}^n a_k converges to L. If the a_k ≥ 0, divergence is denoted by Σ a_k = ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telescoping series, harmonic series divergence examples used to illustrate. Important caution: infinite sum is defined as a limit of partial sums — there is no literal 'adding infinitely many numbers' outside of this limiting process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonnegative-series bounded partial-sums criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For a series Σ a_k with a_k ≥ 0, the series converges if and only if the partial sums are bounded: there exists M such that for every n, a_1 + ... + a_n < M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: monotonicity of partial sums plus completeness yields convergence to sup partial-sum. This motivates writing Σ a_k < ∞ as shorthand for 'series converges to a finite limit' for nonnegative terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute convergence implies convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A series Σ a_k is said to converge absolutely if Σ |a_k| converges; absolute convergence implies ordinary convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard sufficient condition to guarantee convergence independent of order; contrasts with conditional convergence where rearrangement can change sums (series addition not commutative).
